review.note: One independent agent's blind review and passage-hidden pass, with a re-review on 2026-10-08 (docs/reviews/2026-10-07-reading-level-items-review.md); S1–S7 reviewer-authored and author-checked. Not item statistics or human approval; see docs/reading-level.md.

probes.intro: A short fable about a fox and a stork.

items.stem: What did the Fox give the Stork for dinner?
options: A dinner in a jar with a long neck
Soup in a very shallow dish
An empty dish with no soup in it
Soup that was far too hot to eat
items.rationale: The Fox “put nothing before her but some soup in a very shallow dish.”

items.stem: Why could the Fox not eat at the Stork’s house?
options: The Stork served him a very shallow dish
The Stork ate the dinner before he could start
He was still angry about the joke
His snout would not fit into the narrow jar
items.rationale: The dinner was in a jar “in which the Fox could not insert his snout.”

items.stem: What does the Stork mean when she says, “One bad turn deserves another”?
options: She tricked the Fox because he tricked her first
She is sorry that her dinner went badly
She wants the Fox to cook her a better dinner next time
Friends should take turns cooking dinner for each other
items.rationale: The Fox served the soup “for a joke” that the Stork could not eat, so she served a dinner the Fox could not reach.

probes.intro: A science writer describes the inside of a honeybee hive.

items.stem: Why does the air inside the hive need to be moved?
options: Rain has come in through the open windows of the hive
The honey has started to spoil
The crowded bees make it hot and the air bad
The nurse bees need cool air for the young bees
items.rationale: Where “so many insects are packed closely together the heat will become very great, and the air impure and unwholesome.”

items.stem: The bees wave their wings to make “a current of air.” What is a current of air?
options: Air that is moving along
Air that is here right now
Air that smells sweet like honey
A small cloud of dust
items.rationale: The bees wave their wings “to and fro, producing a current of air,” and so “air is sent into all the passages.”

items.stem: Why do more bees stand all over the floor of the hive, fanning with their backs to the entrance?
options: To keep the honey collectors from coming in
To cool the honey before it is stored
To guard the hive from other insects
To send the fresh air farther into the hive
items.rationale: Together with the bees at the entrance they fan, “and in this way air is sent into all the passages.”

probes.intro: A story about the writer Oliver Goldsmith, retold for young readers. The hyphens in long words show their parts.

items.stem: What did Goldsmith find when he visited the family?
options: The man had a bad fever and needed medicine
The family had just moved into a new house
The man had no work and there was no food
The woman had already called another doctor
items.rationale: “He was not sick, but in distress; and, as for eating, there was no food in the house.”

items.stem: Goldsmith “had studied to be a phy-si-cian.” What is a physician?
options: A doctor
A writer of books
A poor man
A shopkeeper who sells boxes
items.rationale: He was “called Doctor Goldsmith” because of this study, and he was asked to “go and see her husband, who was sick.”

items.stem: The directions say to take the “medicine” as often as necessity requires. What does Goldsmith mean?
options: Take the medicine three times a day
Bring the box back when he is well
Save the money until he is sick again
Use the money whenever you need it
items.rationale: The heavy box “was full of pieces of money,” so the medicine was the money itself.

probes.intro: A fairy tale from the Brothers Grimm about a servant girl and the elves.
probes.contentNote: The story ends with news that the maid’s master and mistress have died while she was away; there is no death scene.

items.stem: Why did the maid take the letter to her master and mistress?
options: She thought the letter was meant for them
She could not read it herself
She was afraid to open a letter from elves
She needed their leave to stop sweeping
items.rationale: “as she could not read, she laid her broom in the corner” and took the letter to them.

items.stem: The maid was “very cleanly and industrious.” What does industrious mean?
options: Hard-working
Working in a factory
Clean and tidy
Poor and hungry
items.rationale: She “swept down the house every day” and was about to begin her work.

items.stem: Why did the maid agree to go with the elves?
options: Her master and mistress told her that she had to go
The elves had promised to fill both her pockets with gold
She wanted to see the inside of a mountain
She had heard that no one should say no to the elves
items.rationale: “as she was told that no one ought to refuse the elves anything, she made up her mind to go.”

probes.intro: Jack, a boy, has been carried to Fairyland by an albatross, a large sea bird. There he travels with Mopsa, a young fairy, and an old apple-woman.

items.stem: What does the apple-woman say when Jack asks where the Queen is?
options: The Queen is asleep in the boat
The Queen has gone back to Jack’s world
The Queen will be back after they eat breakfast
Asking questions is not done in Fairyland
items.rationale: She answers, “It’s not the fashion to ask questions in Fairyland.”

items.stem: Why are none of Jack’s people in Fairyland, according to Mopsa?
options: The albatross took him far away to another world
The albatross took him back before people existed
His people are hiding in the border country
Fairies do not allow people into the real Fairylands
items.rationale: The albatross “did not fly with you a long way off, but a long way back,” to when people “are not made yet.”

items.stem: Mopsa thought that not knowing her letters “did not signify.” What does signify mean here?
options: Matter
Make a sign
Spell out
Surprise
items.rationale: Jack says “How ashamed I am” that she does not know her letters, but she simply goes off to play.

items.stem: Why does the apple-woman say that Mopsa is “talking so queen-like already”?
options: Mopsa has just been crowned queen of the fairies
Mopsa is giving orders to the apple-woman and Jack
Mopsa explains things the way grown-up fairies do
Mopsa is pretending to be the missing Queen
items.rationale: She says it is “just what the grown-up fairies say,” and tells Mopsa to “explain it to him.”

probes.intro: A nature-study writer describes frogs she has watched.

items.stem: “The eyes of frogs are very prominent.” What does prominent mean here?
options: Standing out, easy to see
Important and well known
Small and hard to find
Closed most of the time
items.rationale: The frog can draw “its eyes back into its head,” and its eyes can “shine up and attract pursuers.”

items.stem: Why is it useful for a frog to be green while a toad is the color of soil?
options: Green frogs are easier for enemies to find
Toads are older than frogs
Each one matches the place where it lives
Frogs need more sunlight than toads
items.rationale: “the frog lives among green things, while it is to the toad’s advantage to be the color of the soil.”

items.stem: In which frog is the ear larger than the eye?
options: The green frog
The leopard frog
The tree frog
The bullfrog
items.rationale: “in the bullfrog, is larger than the eye.”

items.stem: Why does the leopard frog at the bottom of the aquarium let its eyelids fall over its eyes?
options: Because it is falling asleep
So its eyes will not shine and give it away
So it can change the color of its shining eyes
So it can hear better under water
items.rationale: It covers its eyes “so that they do not shine up and attract pursuers.”

probes.intro: In this nature book from 1903, a writer talks with a group of children about dragonflies.
probes.contentNote: Birds eat some young dragonflies in this passage.

items.stem: What does the larva do just before it changes into a dragonfly?
options: It climbs out of the water on a weed or stick
It swims down to the deepest part of the pond
It spins a silk case around its body
It eats as many mosquitoes as it can
items.rationale: “It climbs up a weed or a stick until it is clear out of the water.”

items.stem: “They seem to come in swarms.” What are swarms?
options: Warm sunny days
Pairs that stay together
Big moving crowds
Long straight lines
items.rationale: Dragonflies are seen “darting about in every direction” where “there are many gnats and mosquitoes.”

items.stem: Why is the time just after the dragonfly leaves its old skin its “hour of danger”?
options: It is still too small to find any food
Fish can easily reach it on the stick
The sun may dry it out before it moves
Its new wings are not yet ready to fly
items.rationale: Birds have eaten them “before the flabby little wings had grown stiff.”

items.stem: Why does the writer tell the story of the men who raised dragonflies?
options: To show how easily dragonflies can be tamed by people
To show that raising them against mosquitoes fails
To explain how the larva changes into a dragonfly
To prove that birds eat many young dragonflies
items.rationale: As soon as they had wings, the dragonflies flew off “without stopping to catch a single mosquito.”

probes.intro: In this nature book from 1903, a writer and a group of children look at caddis-fly larvae in a brook. The book spells the name “caddice.”
probes.contentNote: Some insects in this passage eat other insects.

items.stem: What do some caddice larvae use for their cases besides sand?
options: Mud, feathers, or bits of bark
A silk tube spun from their mouths
Twigs, leaves, or tiny snail shells
Pebbles, moss, or fish scales
items.rationale: “They stick little twigs together, and some use little pieces of leaves,” and others “use tiny snail shells.”

items.stem: “Notice the tracery in the soft mud of the brook.” What is tracery?
options: A set of footprints
A pattern of thin lines
A pile of loose sand
A small hole or a burrow
items.rationale: The lines “look as though some one had been ornamenting the bottom of the brook.”

items.stem: How does the larva hold on to its case while pulling it?
options: With its strong front legs
With sticky threads from its mouth
By wedging its hard head inside
With tiny hooks at its tail end
items.rationale: It has “a pair of tiny hooks at the tail end by which it can hold on to the silk lining.”

items.stem: Why, according to the writer, might caddice larvae build such strong cases?
options: To stop May fly larvae eating them back
To keep warm in the cold water
To carry the food they have caught
To hide from the children who look for them
items.rationale: They eat May fly larvae and build strong cases “to prevent the May fly larvae from returning the compliment.”

probes.intro: In this chapter of a novel, Mary, a girl who has come from India to live in a large house in England, has found an old key.

items.stem: Why does Mary want to see inside the closed garden?
options: She wants to pick roses for her room
Someone in the house has asked her to look
It has been closed for so many years
She thinks the key was left there for her
items.rationale: “It was because it had been shut up so long that she wanted to see it.”

items.stem: What does the narrator suggest is changing Mary?
options: The moor air and her lonely free time
The servants are teaching her new games
Kind friends in the house are cheering her up
Missing India makes her think about the past
items.rationale: Being alone “was actually awakening her imagination,” and the moor air “had a great deal to do with it.”

items.stem: “The ivy was the baffling thing.” What does baffling mean here?
options: Thick and tangled
Hard to figure out
Beautiful and shiny
Dangerous to touch
items.rationale: However carefully she looked, she saw only leaves, and it seemed silly “to be near it and not be able to get in.”

items.stem: Why does the passage end with Mary deciding to carry the key whenever she goes out?
options: It shows she fears that someone will take the key from her
It shows she means to try it in the closed rooms of the house
It shows she wants to make up a game of her own with it
It shows she means to keep looking for the door
items.rationale: She will carry it “so that if she ever should find the hidden door she would be ready.”

probes.intro: In this retelling of a Greek myth, the heroes of the ship Argo sail into an unknown sea. (Hellens are Greeks.)

items.stem: Why were the heroes afraid as they sailed into the Black Sea?
options: Their ship had been badly damaged in a storm on the way
No Greek had crossed it, and strange stories were told of it
Orpheus had told them that the goddess Hera was against them
They had run short of food and water on the voyage
items.rationale: “No Hellen had ever crossed it,” and people “told strange stories of it.”

items.stem: Tiphys is called “the cunning helmsman.” What does cunning mean here?
options: Dishonest and sly
Frightened and weak
Proud and boastful
Skillful and clever
items.rationale: Tiphys watches until he can follow the heron, which he calls “the cunning bird,” through the one gap.

items.stem: Why does Tiphys stand silent before steering between the rocks?
options: He has decided to turn the ship around
He is angry with Orpheus for frightening the crew
He is watching for a sign of a safe way through
He is waiting for the rocks to sink
items.rationale: He stood silent “till he saw a heron” that seemed to be “looking for a passage through,” then followed it.

items.stem: Why does the author say the rocks struck “but a feather from his tail”?
options: To show how narrowly the heron escaped
To show that the heron was badly hurt
To explain why the heron left the ship
To show that the rocks were made of glass
items.rationale: The rocks “clashed together as the bird fled swiftly through,” missing it by only a feather.

probes.intro: This fairy tale begins at a royal wedding in a king’s castle.

items.stem: Why was doubling the Page’s salary “not of much use to him”?
options: The King took the order back the next day
He had to share it with the other pages
It was paid only in white and red roses
He was not paid any salary at all
items.rationale: “As he received no salary at all this was not of much use to him.”

items.stem: What does the King’s flute-playing show about his court?
options: People flatter the King instead of being honest
The court cares more for music than for dancing
The King is a gifted musician who can play by ear
The Princess is too shy to say what she thinks
items.rationale: He “played very badly, but no one had ever dared to tell him so,” and everyone cried, “Charming! charming!”

items.stem: “exclaimed a pensive Catherine Wheel.” What does pensive mean here?
options: Spinning round and round
Proud and boastful
Sadly thoughtful
Brightly colored
items.rationale: She remembers a love “in early life,” prides herself on her broken heart, and murmurs that “Romance is dead.”

items.stem: How does the narrator comment on the Catherine Wheel’s view that “Romance is dead”?
options: By showing that the other fireworks agree with her
By noting that repeating a thing does not make it true
By explaining that she is the oldest firework there
By hinting that the bride does not really love the Prince
items.rationale: She is “one of those people who think that, if you say the same thing over and over a great many times, it becomes true in the end.”

probes.intro: A naturalist describes collecting insects for three weeks in 1855–56 at a cottage on a forested mountain in Borneo. The table lists what he caught each night.
probes.contentNote: The collector catches and pins moths for study.

items.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Moths are easiest to catch near towns and villages
His catch depended on weather and on his house
Bright moonlight helps moths find a lamp at night
A collector should study ferns rather than insects
items.rationale: Most moths came on “very wet and dark nights,” and he never again had “a low boarded and whitewashed verandah.”

items.stem: According to the table, what kind of night brought the most moths?
options: Fine nights with clear moonlight
Cloudy nights with a few showers
Rainy nights with moonlight
Dark nights with heavy rain
items.rationale: “more than 800 of them were collected on four very wet and dark nights.”

items.stem: Lights in other houses were “a counter-attraction.” What is a counter-attraction?
options: A rival pull drawing them elsewhere
A light that frightens insects off
A shop counter where insects are sold
A second lamp to help the collector
items.rationale: Living among “other houses whose lights were a counter-attraction” kept him from collecting moths.

items.stem: Why does the writer end by suggesting that naturalists carry a white verandah or tent?
options: To shelter from the heavy rain while they work
To keep insects out of their sleeping rooms
To recreate the conditions of his one success
To display the moths after they are caught
items.rationale: He never again lived in “a solitary jungle-house with a low boarded and whitewashed verandah,” and calls such an apparatus required.

probes.intro: A boy in India and his young elephant, Kari, are visiting the crowded city of Benares. Their pet monkey, Kopee, has waited for them outside the city.
probes.contentNote: The elephant kills a dog in this passage, though the boy tries to stop him.

items.stem: Why does the narrator turn down the goldsmith’s rings?
options: He cannot afford the price of the gold rings
He fears that the rings would hurt Kari’s brand-new tusks
He would rather buy silver rings than gold ones
He thinks the young tusks are too beautiful to spoil
items.rationale: He says the tusks are “too beautiful to spoil with rings yet.”

items.stem: Why does Kari walk straight into the river after leaving the city?
options: He seems to be hot and tired from the long walk through town
He seems to be trying to wash away the wrong he has done
He wants a long drink of water after his big meal
He is hiding from the dogs that chased him
items.rationale: The narrator says Kari knew “he had done something wrong and he was trying to cleanse himself of it.”

items.stem: “The less attention he paid to them, the more audacious the dogs grew.” What does audacious mean?
options: Easy to hear
Frightened and shy
Bold and daring
Tired and very hungry
items.rationale: The dogs “came after us” until “we were hemmed in by packs of dogs.”

items.stem: Why does the narrator tell the goldsmith that Kari “will live more than one hundred and twenty-five years”?
options: To say the goldsmith will be dead before Kari wears gold
To explain why Kari’s tusks have just started to grow
To ask for rings strong enough to last that long
To show that Kari is much older than he looks
items.rationale: He adds, “thou shalt be dead by then, and so there will be no chance of soiling his ivory by buying thy gold.”

probes.intro: Zitkala-Ša, a Dakota writer, recalls her first day teaching at an eastern school for Native American children after an illness interrupted her college studies.
probes.contentNote: The narrator has been seriously ill. The passage uses some historical words for race.

items.stem: Why did the narrator not go home to her mother after her illness?
options: Her mother had written asking her to stay and work in the East
She had no money for the long trip West
She was too proud to face what her mother would say
Her college would not allow her to leave
items.rationale: “my pride kept me from returning to my mother,” whose rebuke “would have been unbearable.”

items.stem: What does the narrator sense in her employer’s reaction to her?
options: He is disappointed by how small and worn she looks
He is angry that she has arrived so late
He is delighted to finally meet her
He is worried that her room is too small and plain for her
items.rationale: After his eye “measured my height and breadth,” she heard “a subtle note of disappointment in his voice.”

items.stem: She met “the imposing figure of a stately gray-haired man.” What does imposing mean here?
options: Forcing others to obey
Kind and gentle
Old and bent over
Large and impressive
items.rationale: She was “awed by his wondrous height and his strong square shoulders.”

items.stem: She felt “as if years of weariness lay like water-soaked logs upon me.” What does this comparison suggest?
options: She is wet and cold from her long journey
Her tiredness feels like a heavy, crushing weight
She feels calm, as if floating on water
She longs to be back home among the forests of the West
items.rationale: The image follows “a leaden weakness came over me,” and she throws herself on the bed.

probes.intro: Mary Austin writes about a spring in the California desert, the birds that visit it, and old marks on the land nearby.

items.stem: The road-runner crouches until he “looked most like some bright venomous snake.” Why does the author make this comparison?
options: To show that road-runners like to hunt and eat snakes
To explain why the sparrows bathe in dust
To show that he is afraid of the water
To show how threatening he makes himself look
items.rationale: He takes this shape while “daunting them with shrill abuse and feint of battle.”

items.stem: At noon the hawks keep “a truce to all hostilities because of the heat.” What does truce mean here?
options: A shared drink at the spring
A loud warning call
A pause in fighting
A safe hiding place
items.rationale: In the heat the hawks are “sitting panting, with wings aslant,” not hunting the other birds.

items.stem: How does the Shoshone water sign show the way to the spring?
options: An arrow laid in the gap would point to the spring
Its stones are piled higher on the spring’s side
Its wavy carved lines measure the distance to walk
It is built right beside the spring itself
items.rationale: If an arrow were placed in the opening, “it would point as the crow flies to the spring.”

items.stem: What does the writer say about the pictures and symbols carved around the spring?
options: They show how many days it is to the next spring
People living there now do not know what they mean
The Shoshones carved them to mark their trails
They warn travellers to stay away from the spring
items.rationale: The rock is “scored over with strange pictures and symbols that have no meaning to the Indians of the present day.”

probes.intro: Mary Austin writes about the high Sierra mountains of California at the start of winter.
probes.contentNote: Some wild animals are weak and hungry in deep snow.

items.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to stay safe in a mountain snowstorm
How the season’s snows come and how living things respond
Why the valley gets more snow than the peaks
How birds fly south before the first winter storms arrive
items.rationale: It moves from “the great snows that come at the beginning of winter” to later drifts, the yearly “big snow,” and the silver fir.

items.stem: Why do only Clark’s crow and the jays “make light of” the coming storm?
options: They are too young to know about storms
They have already flown south for the winter
Their cries are what bring the warning wind
They are hardy enough not to need shelter
items.rationale: “only they can afford to,” while the wind cries the other wild creatures “to their holes.”

items.stem: Before the snow, “the sky glowers.” What does glowers mean here?
options: Glows brightly
Clears up again
Looks threatening
Turns a soft pink
items.rationale: The pine-trees creak “although there is no wind,” and “It grows chill, blind clouds fumble in the cañons.”

items.stem: How does the silver fir handle a heavy load of snow?
options: Its branches droop, drop the snow, and spring back
Its branches snap off under the weight
It sheds its needles before the snow
It grows taller each year to stay above the deep drifts
items.rationale: “there is a soft sough and muffled dropping, the boughs recover, and the weighting goes on.”

probes.intro: Frederick Douglass, then enslaved in Baltimore, had been badly beaten by workers at Mr. Gardner’s shipyard. Calking means sealing the seams of a ship.

items.stem: “Master Hugh, finding he could get no redress, refused to let me go back again to Mr. Gardner.” What does redress mean here?
options: A new set of work clothes
Permission to leave the city of Baltimore
A remedy or payment for a wrong
An apology from Douglass
items.rationale: Douglass had been hurt at Gardner’s yard, so “his wife dressed my wound,” and Hugh could get nothing to set that wrong right.

items.stem: How did Douglass’s working life change after he learned to calk?
options: He worked at Master Hugh’s yard, where Hugh set his wages
He found his own jobs and contracts and collected his pay
He earned less than the other calkers
He was sent back to Mr. Gardner’s shipyard
items.rationale: “I sought my own employment, made my own contracts, and collected the money which I earned.”

items.stem: What does Douglass conclude about how better conditions affected him?
options: They made him content to remain enslaved
They made him think less about freedom
They made him trust Master Hugh more than before
They made him want freedom more, not feel content
items.rationale: “whenever my condition was improved, instead of its increasing my contentment, it only increased my desire to be free.”

items.stem: Why does Douglass list “Not because he earned it,—not because he had any hand in earning it”?
options: To rule out every justification, leaving only force
To repeat the reasons Hugh gave for taking his wages
To show that the shipyard paid its calkers unfairly
To admit that he still owed Master Hugh some money
items.rationale: After the list he concludes that Hugh took the money “solely because he had the power to compel me to give it up.”

probes.intro: Benjamin Franklin recalls teaching himself languages as an adult. His eighteenth-century spellings, such as “us'd” for “used,” are kept.

items.stem: How did Franklin and his acquaintance use chess to study Italian?
options: They spoke Italian to each other while they played
The winner of each game set the loser a study task
The loser paid for the winner’s lessons
They gave up chess to have more time to study
items.rationale: “the victor in every game should have a right to impose a task” of grammar or translation.

items.stem: Why did Franklin understand more Latin than he expected?
options: He had studied Latin for many years as a boy
The Latin Testament included a translation
His chess partner had been secretly teaching him Latin
French, Italian, and Spanish had prepared him for it
items.rationale: He found he did better because “those preceding languages had greatly smooth'd my way.”

items.stem: Why does Franklin point out that “we do not begin with the Greek”?
options: To show the usual argument for Latin first is inconsistent
To recommend that students begin with Greek before Latin
To explain why he himself did not study Greek at school
To prove that Greek is an easier language than Latin
items.rationale: He sees “some inconsistency in our common mode of teaching languages”: Latin comes first to ease the modern tongues, “and yet we do not begin with the Greek.”

items.stem: What does Franklin suggest to those in charge of educating young people?
options: Begin with Greek so that learning Latin is easier later
Teach languages to fewer students
Consider teaching modern languages before Latin
Use games like chess to teach Latin
items.rationale: He asks whether “it would not have been better to have begun with the French, proceeding to the Italian.”

probes.intro: Booker T. Washington recalls his boyhood in West Virginia after emancipation, when he worked in a salt furnace and then a coal mine.

items.stem: How did Washington get most of his boyhood education?
options: In evening classes after work
At day school, with a trained teacher
From books that his mother bought him
From the miners who worked beside him
items.rationale: “the greater part of the education I secured in my boyhood was gathered through the night-school after my day's work was done.”

items.stem: What does Washington see as the worst effect of mine work on young boys?
options: It leaves their skin dirty and very hard to clean
It pays them less than it pays adults
It stunts them and takes away their ambition
It forces them to move far from home
items.rationale: “what is worse,” such boys are often “physically and mentally dwarfed” and “soon lose ambition.”

items.stem: How does Washington come to measure success?
options: Mostly by the high position a person reaches
By how many years of schooling a person has completed
By the family a person is born into
More by hardships overcome than by rank reached
items.rationale: “success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome.”

items.stem: How does the paragraph beginning “In later years” relate to the one before it?
options: It adds more details about the coal mine
It revises the boyhood envy he just described
It repeats the same view about envy in stronger words
It tells what became of the orphan boy
items.rationale: Having described how he “used to envy the white boy,” he writes, “I do not envy the white boy as I once did.”

probes.intro: Near the end of a novel, Jim, now a grown man, has visited his old friend Ántonia and her family on their farm. He returns to the prairie town where he grew up.
probes.contentNote: Jim learns that some old friends have died.

items.stem: Why, according to Ambrosch, might Leo have run off into the pasture?
options: He had been sent ahead to open the lane gate
He is sorry Jim is leaving, or jealous of him
He wanted to go hunting up on the Niobrara
He meant to wave goodbye from the windmill
items.rationale: His brother says, “Maybe he’s sorry to have you go, and maybe he’s jealous.”

items.stem: The boy smiled at Jim “with unabashed pleasure and affection.” What does unabashed mean here?
options: Shy and bashful
Not embarrassed
Hidden and secret
Puzzled and unsure
items.rationale: After Jim’s “Oh, yes you do!” the boy, who had been “blushing,” simply smiles at him as he drives away.

items.stem: Why does Jim feel “at home again” in the rough pastures north of town?
options: His grandparents’ old house still stands out in those pastures
He meets old friends walking out there
The land there was never ploughed and looks as it once did
The fields remind him of the city where he now lives
items.rationale: The land “had never been ploughed up, and the long red grass of early times still grew shaggy.”

items.stem: What does the old road come to mean to Jim at the end of the passage?
options: A tie to Ántonia that their childhood still holds
A sign that he was wrong to leave the prairie
A reminder that old ways are best forgotten
A route he plans to travel with the Cuzak boys next summer
items.rationale: He understands “the same road was to bring us together again,” for “we possessed together the precious, the incommunicable past.”

probes.intro: In this section of an 1837 address, Ralph Waldo Emerson discusses the scholar’s education.
probes.contentNote: This 1837 address uses nineteenth-century gendered language.

items.stem: According to the passage, how does a young mind’s understanding of nature develop?
options: It learns general laws first, then notices each separate thing
It studies books first, then turns to nature
It classifies things, then forgets the classes
It sees things as separate, then joins them under shared laws
items.rationale: “To the young mind everything is individual,” but “By and by it finds how to join two things and see in them one nature.”

items.stem: “The ambitious soul sits down before each refractory fact.” What does refractory mean here?
options: Bending light, as a lens or prism does
Recently discovered by science
Stubborn; hard to explain or classify
Of little importance to the mind
items.rationale: The soul “reduces all strange constitutions, all new powers, to their class and their law,” so a refractory fact is one that resists that order.

items.stem: Of nature and the soul, Emerson writes, “One is seal and one is print.” What relationship does this image express?
options: They correspond exactly, like a stamp and its mark
Nature is a book that the soul must print and read
The soul is sealed away from nature and cannot touch it
Nature copies the soul, but poorly
items.rationale: Just before the image he says nature is the soul’s opposite, “answering to it part for part.”

items.stem: What does Emerson conclude in the final sentences?
options: Science should replace the study of the self
Self-knowledge and the study of the world become a single aim
The mind can understand just a small part of nature
Ancient wisdom matters much more than modern science does
items.rationale: The precepts “Know thyself” and “Study nature” “become at last one maxim.”

probes.intro: This passage comes from Walden (1854), Henry David Thoreau’s book about the two years he spent living in a cabin in the woods.
probes.contentNote: Thoreau’s judgments about who reads well are his own opinions, from 1854.

items.stem: What does Thoreau claim about real reading in the final paragraph?
options: It takes hard effort at our sharpest hours
It should give way to direct experience
It matters less than knowing how to keep accounts
It comes easily once a person knows the alphabet
items.rationale: True reading is “what we have to stand on tiptoe to read and devote our most alert and wakeful hours to.”

items.stem: Thoreau says most people read the great poets “as the multitude read the stars, at most astrologically, not astronomically.” What does this suggest?
options: They read poetry mostly at night, by the light of the stars
They prefer the science of astronomy to reading poetry
They read mainly poems about the stars
They read for fanciful meanings, not with careful study
items.rationale: He contrasts such reading with reading as “a noble intellectual exercise,” of which most men “know little or nothing.”

items.stem: Why, according to Thoreau, does the wealthy trader work to give his children intellectual culture?
options: He wants his children to become traders too
He feels his riches cannot replace the culture he lacks
He has read the classics himself and wants to share them
Society expects it of wealthy families
items.rationale: The trader feels “the vanity and insufficiency of all his riches” and the culture “whose want he so keenly feels.”

items.stem: “Most men have learned to read to serve a paltry convenience.” What does paltry mean?
options: Practical and useful
Ancient and respected
Small and unimportant
Strict and required
items.rationale: Thoreau sets this use beside learning “to cipher in order to keep accounts,” a minor aim next to reading as “a noble intellectual exercise.”

probes.intro: In this dialogue from Plato’s Republic (Benjamin Jowett’s translation), Socrates, who narrates (“I said”), discusses with Glaucon which studies train the mind.

items.stem: What does Socrates argue arithmetic is truly for?
options: Helping soldiers count and arrange their troops
Testing whether our senses judge size and weight correctly
Drawing the mind past appearances to what is real
Training people to keep accounts in trade
items.rationale: “the true use of it is simply to draw the soul toward being.”

items.stem: Why does Socrates use the example of three fingers?
options: To contrast clear sense reports with confused ones
To show that the eye cannot tell one finger from another
To prove that the middle finger is the largest of the three
To explain how painters use light and shade
items.rationale: Each “equally appears a finger,” which invites no thought, but sight sees their greatness and smallness “only in a confused manner.”

items.stem: Why, according to Socrates, does seeing a finger as both great and small “invite thought”?
options: The finger looks different when seen from near and from far
The sight cannot see fingers clearly in poor light
Thought is needed to decide what a finger is
The senses report opposites at once, which puzzles the mind
items.rationale: The soul is “perplexed” by such reports and “summons to her aid calculation and intelligence.”

items.stem: “the sight never intimates to the mind that a finger is other than a finger.” What does intimates mean here?
options: Becomes close friends with
Suggests or signals
Hides something from
Argues against
items.rationale: The sense of touch likewise “only intimates to the soul that the same thing is felt to be both hard and soft.”

probes.intro: In this chapter of The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Bertrand Russell asks what knowledge is. His examples refer to British prime ministers and newspapers of his day.

items.stem: Why does Russell reject defining knowledge simply as “true belief”?
options: Hardly any of our beliefs turn out to be true
A belief can be true by luck or come from a false belief
Knowledge needs an official source, such as a telegram report
True beliefs are usually reached by valid reasoning
items.rationale: Readers of a lucky newspaper forecast believe the right result, but “they cannot be said to have knowledge.”

items.stem: What does the example about Socrates being a Greek illustrate?
options: False premisses can still make a perfectly valid argument
Historical facts about the life of Socrates are uncertain
A true conclusion is not knowledge if it does not follow
Intuitive knowledge cannot be defined
items.rationale: Though premisses and conclusion are true, “the conclusion does not follow from the premisses.”

items.stem: Why does Russell call the definition “knowledge is what is validly deduced from known premisses” circular?
options: It uses the idea of knowing to define knowing
It returns at the end to the example it began with
It covers too many cases
It depends on a false belief
items.rationale: He says “it assumes that we already know what is meant by” known premisses.

items.stem: What does Russell conclude about the idea of knowledge at the end of the passage?
options: It can be defined exactly as deduction from known premisses
It is the same thing as true belief
It covers intuitive knowledge but not derivative knowledge
Its edges are blurred, so an exact definition would mislead
items.rationale: “knowledge” “is not a precise conception: it merges into” probable opinion, and a precise definition “must be more or less misleading.”
